property_summary: For any caller address X and target _owner, only the original admin (deployer) can change C.owner via setOwner; the mutant removing onlyAdmin allows other callers to change owner so for some X != admin the owner will differ.

For all callers, calling setOwner updates C.owner() iff the caller is the admin (the original contract enforces admin-only updates); the mutant that requires msg.sender == owner instead will sometimes prevent admin from changing owner and thus break this property for some inputs.

For any caller address, when the original contract's admin calls setOwner(x) the owner becomes x; the mutant wrongly additionally requires msg.sender==owner so some admin calls that should succeed will instead fail or leave owner unchanged.

For any address newOwner and any caller actor, when the admin calls setOwner(newOwner) the contract's owner becomes newOwner (reference preserves admin-only ability to set owner); the mutant that also requires msg.sender == owner breaks this because admin calls will fail unless admin==owner, so for some fuzzed actor/newOwner the owner will not change.

For any fuzzed addresses (adminCaller, newOwner) when the contract's admin (the deployer) calls setOwner(newOwner) the public owner getter must equal newOwner after the call; the mutant that additionally requires msg.sender==owner prevents admin from changing owner when admin != owner and thus violates this rule for some inputs.

For every address newOwner, when the admin (the deployer) calls setOwner(newOwner) the contract's public owner becomes newOwner (the reference always allows the admin to update owner; the mutant sometimes blocks this by requiring the caller be the current owner).

For all callers, only the deployer-admin can successfully call setOwner; the mutant inverts the require so some non-admin caller can (or the admin cannot) change owner, so there exists an input caller for which owner differs between reference and mutant.

For all callers, only the admin address can successfully call setOwner and change owner; the mutant that allows owner as an additional privileged caller violates this by permitting owner to call setOwner and thus change owner in some cases.

For every caller address, only the original admin (the deployer) can successfully change owner via setOwner; the mutant also lets the current owner perform that action, which breaks the rule when caller == owner != admin.

For every caller address, only the original admin (the deployer) can successfully change C.owner via setOwner; the mutant additionally allows the current owner to change owner, violating this rule when caller == owner != admin.
For any caller who is admin, calling setOwner(...) completes and returns true in the reference implementation; the mutant returns false for some inputs (admin caller), breaking this rule.

For every caller address, calling setOwner(...) on the reference either reverts for non-admins and returns true for the admin; the mutant allows non-admin calls to succeed and return true, so there exists some caller (any non-admin) and owner argument where reference reverts but mutant returns true.

For any caller who is admin, calling setOwner(x) always updates the public owner to x (the reference sets owner to the passed address; the mutant returns early and leaves owner unchanged for some inputs).

For every caller and input, calling setOwner(...) on the correct contract C always updates the public owner to the supplied address (owner == _owner) while the mutant assigns to admin instead and therefore for some fuzzed _owner the public owner will not equal the supplied address after the call.

Only the admin (deployer) can successfully change owner via setOwner; the mutant removes that restriction allowing non-admin callers to change owner (so there exists some caller/address for which setOwner succeeds on mutant but would be rejected on the reference).
